hook_text: Load-shedding hits. The lights die. Here is where every bit of your energy really comes from.
clip_script: The lights go off. Most of South Africa's electricity comes from burning coal, a fossil fuel made from plants that died millions of years ago and were squashed underground. Oil and gas formed the same way. We are burning millions of years of fuel in a few centuries, so it will run out, and burning it makes smoke and heats the planet. That is non-renewable. Nuclear uses uranium dug from the ground: almost no smoke, but dangerous waste. Now look at the windowsill. A little solar light, charged by the Sun all day. Sunlight, wind and flowing water get refilled by nature every day. That is renewable. The catch: the Sun sets and the wind drops. And the twist? Even coal's energy was sunlight once, trapped by ancient plants.
visual_style: Whiteboard house going dark; a coal lump unpeeling into ancient ferns; a timeline of millions of years squeezed into a sliver; a sunny windowsill light glowing; wind turbines spinning.
mood: Relatable everyday problem with a big-picture twist.
pacing: Dark opener, a fast fossil-fuel history, a bright renewable turn, a clever final twist.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and trace every energy source back to where it came from.
